market_context: United States/general English; lean-to-fat percentages on ground meat labels and cooked-versus-raw composition
title: What the fat percentage on ground meat means

seo.title: Ground meat fat percentage: what 90/10 and 80/20 mean
seo.meta_description: A 90/10 label means roughly 90% lean and 10% fat by raw weight. Cooking removes water and some fat, so 100 g cooked does not necessarily contain exactly 10 g fat.
seo.search_intent: Understand what 95/5, 90/10 and 80/20 mean on ground meat and how the percentages relate to calories after cooking.

excerpt: A 90/10 label describes the raw mixture: roughly 90% lean tissue and 10% fat by weight. It does not mean 100 g cooked meat will contain exactly 10 g fat, because cooking changes both water and fat content.
content_html:
Labels such as 95/5, 90/10 and 80/20 describe the lean-to-fat ratio of raw ground meat. A 90/10 product is approximately 90% lean and 10% fat by raw weight. It does not mean that 100 g of the cooked meat will contain exactly 10 g fat.

What common ratios represent

LabelDeclared raw fatFat in 200 g raw product
95/55%~10 g
93/77%~14 g
90/1010%~20 g
85/1515%~30 g
80/2020%~40 g

Moving from 95/5 to 80/20 adds 15 g fat per 100 g raw meat. At about 9 calories per gram of fat, that represents up to roughly 135 additional calories per 100 g before accounting for cooking losses.

Why cooked nutrition does not match the package ratio

Cooking removes water, and some rendered fat may drain into the pan. The final food weighs less. That is why 90/10 ground beef can show around 12 g fat per 100 g in a cooked composition table: the meat did not gain fat; water loss concentrated what remained.

Whether rendered fat is drained or retained in a sauce also changes the amount eaten.

Lean percentage is not the same as calorie percentage

An 80/20 product is 20% fat by weight, not 20% of calories from fat. Because fat provides 9 calories per gram while protein provides about 4, fat contributes a much larger share of total energy than its weight percentage suggests.

More lean tissue usually means more protein per raw ounce

When fat is replaced by lean muscle, raw protein concentration generally rises. After cooking, water loss can concentrate protein further, which is why very lean cooked ground meats can exceed 30 g protein per 100 g.

Fat percentage changes cooking behavior

An 80/20 burger usually releases more rendered fat and tends to remain juicier at the same degree of cooking. A 95/5 patty contains much less fat and can dry out faster when overcooked. The “best” ratio therefore depends on both the recipe and the nutrition goal.

What to compare at the store

Use the lean/fat ratio to compare similar raw products. For actual calories in your meal, check the Nutrition Facts panel and serving size, then remember that cooking yield can change the final weight. A 4-ounce raw patty does not remain 4 ounces after cooking.

Bottom line

Read 90/10 as a description of the raw mixture, not a promise that cooked meat contains exactly 10% fat by final weight. Lean percentage is excellent for comparing purchases; cooked nutrition should be estimated from a matching cooked reference or the product's own instructions and yield.

faq.question: What does 90/10 ground beef mean?
faq.answer: It means the raw mixture is approximately 90% lean tissue and 10% fat by weight.

faq.question: Does 90/10 meat have 10 g fat per 100 g cooked?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Cooking removes water and some rendered fat, changing the final concentration per 100 g.

faq.question: Is 80/20 meat 20% of calories from fat?
faq.answer: No. The 20% refers to weight. Because fat is more calorie-dense than protein, the share of calories from fat is much higher than 20%.
